# About Uchit Vyas

URL: https://hellouchit.com/about/

Uchit Vyas: lead forward deployed engineer in Melbourne. Career from 2011, five books, a US machine-learning patent and 30+ talks.

## About.

I’m a lead forward deployed engineer in Melbourne, focused on AI-led enterprise transformation. I work inside the delivery team and build the thing myself, usually against a date that can’t move.

I started in 2011 writing Java and running Linux servers in Ahmedabad. Cloud was new, so I wrote about it: five books for Apress and Packt between 2013 and 2016, mostly about AWS. Then came DevOps and SRE work for banks in Singapore and Thailand, enterprise architecture at KPMG Singapore, and platform and modernisation work across Australia and New Zealand.

Now I spend most of my time on AI in large enterprises: getting agents and AI services into production, and fixing the data and core platforms they depend on. That means giving an agent its own identity, limiting what it can do, keeping a record a regulator will accept, and still shipping on time.

I still build things myself, from prototypes with new AI tools to a product I run on my own. It keeps my advice honest. Outside work I lift weights and write about training after 35. I speak Gujarati, Hindi and English, and a little Spanish.

# Ten controls for AI agents

URL: https://hellouchit.com/agents/

Ten controls to build before an AI agent goes live in a regulated company, with the evidence auditors ask for, mapped to the EU AI Act, NIST and APRA.

## Ten things a regulator will ask to see before your AI agent goes live.

In build order, with the evidence for each.

Score your agents in two minutes
Download as JSON

## Identity first. Everything else attaches to it.

## Start with these

1Agent runs under its own workload identity
2Declared autonomy level per action class
3Full replayable trajectory
4Retrieved and tool-returned content treated as untrusted data

## Then these, once what they need is in place

5Tool authorisation enforced outside the modelNeeds 1 first
6Bounded blast radiusNeeds 1 first
7Named human approval for consequential actionsNeeds 2 first
8Irreversible actions stagedNeeds 2 first
9Provenance across agentsNeeds 3 first
10Cost measured per resolved taskNeeds 3 first

## Each control, mapped to six frameworks.

EU AI ActISO 42001NIST AI RMFAPRA CPS 230NIST 800-53OWASP LLM

1Agent runs under its own workload identity. Maps to EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST 800-53.

Agent runs under its own workload identity, never a human’s or a shared account.

The most common finding in a first agent review is an agent acting as the engineer who deployed it, which makes attribution impossible and revocation a personnel action. This is not a new control. It is workload identity applied to a new kind of workload, and organisations that already solved it for services have most of the work done.

What an auditor will ask for

IAM export showing a distinct principal per agent, with no human user credentials in any agent execution path. Trust policy showing federated identity rather than a static key. An access-revocation test: disable the agent principal and show its tool calls fail within one polling interval.

Check it yourself (read-only, AWS)

aws sts get-caller-identity --query Arn --output text

You should see: An assumed-role ARN for the agent itself: not a human’s, and not one shared with other agents.

Build first

Nothing. You can start today.

Maps to

EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, APRA CPS 234, NIST SP 800-53, ASD Essential 8

2Declared autonomy level per action class. Maps to EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, APRA CPS 230.

Declared autonomy level per action class, enforced at execution and recorded per run.

Autonomy is not a property of the agent; it is a property of each action it can take. Recording the level in force at the time is what lets you answer what it was allowed to do then, rather than what it is allowed to do now. That is the question an investigation actually asks.

What an auditor will ask for

A register of action classes with the autonomy level assigned to each and who approved it. Per-run records showing the level in force at execution time. Evidence that a level change requires review: a config diff with an approver, not a deploy.

Build first

Nothing. You can start today.

Maps to

EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, AU AI Safety Std, APRA CPS 230

3Full replayable trajectory. Maps to EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, APRA CPS 230.

Full replayable trajectory: every tool call, argument, result and the exact context the model saw.

Logging the final output is enough to debug a demo and nothing else. The test of a trajectory record is whether you can replay from step N; if you cannot, you have a description of what happened rather than evidence of it. The same rows serve the audit pack and the eval set.

What an auditor will ask for

A single run exported end to end: assembled context, retrieved document IDs, each tool call with arguments and result, model and prompt version, tokens, cost and latency. A replay of that run from an intermediate step, demonstrating the trace is sufficient to reconstruct rather than merely describe.

Check it yourself (read-only, OpenTelemetry)

curl -s '<otlp-query>/api/traces?service=<agent>&limit=1' | jq '[.data[0].spans[] | select(.operationName|test("tool"))] | length'

You should see: A span per tool call. If the count is zero the trajectory is reconstructed from logs, not recorded.

Build first

Nothing. You can start today.

Maps to

EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, APRA CPS 230, HIPAA

4Retrieved and tool-returned content treated as untrusted data. Maps to EU AI Act, ISO 42001, OWASP LLM.

Retrieved and tool-returned content treated as untrusted data, never as instructions.

Direct prompt injection is widely tested; indirect injection through a retrieved document, a web page or a tool result is where agents actually get compromised, because the payload arrives after the guardrail. Any content an agent retrieves is attacker-influenceable if an attacker can influence the source.

What an auditor will ask for

Red-team results for indirect prompt injection through each retrieval and tool-result path, not only through direct user input. Evidence of structural separation between instruction and retrieved content. Records showing an injected instruction was not acted upon.

Build first

Nothing. You can start today.

Maps to

OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS, EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001

5Tool authorisation enforced outside the model. Maps to EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF, NIST 800-53, OWASP LLM.

Tool authorisation enforced outside the model, by the tool registry.

An agent can only do what its tools permit, so the tool list is the control and the system prompt is a suggestion. Instructions telling a model what it must not do are not a security boundary. They are a request, and retrieved content will eventually contain instructions that contradict them.

What an auditor will ask for

The tool manifest available to the agent per role, exported from config rather than described. Policy decision logs showing allow and deny with a reason for each tool invocation. A negative test: an agent asked to call a tool outside its scope, and the denial recorded.

Build first

1. Agent runs under its own workload identity

Maps to

EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, OWASP LLM Top 10, NIST SP 800-53

6Bounded blast radius. Maps to ISO 42001, APRA CPS 230, NIST 800-53.

Bounded blast radius: step, spend and rate ceilings, plus a tested kill switch.

A loop without a ceiling is a billing incident with a countdown. The kill switch matters more than the ceiling and is almost never tested mid-run. Stopping an agent between steps is easy. Stopping one that is halfway through a multi-call action is the case that matters.

What an auditor will ask for

Configured ceilings per agent for steps, spend and tool-call rate. An incident or game-day record showing the kill switch stopping an agent mid-run, with the time from decision to halt. Evidence that a halted run leaves consistent state.

Check it yourself (read-only, Kubernetes)

kubectl get resourcequota -A -o json | jq -r '.items[] | "\(.metadata.namespace) \(.spec.hard)"'

You should see: A quota on the agent’s namespace. No quota means the ceiling is theoretical.

Build first

1. Agent runs under its own workload identity

Maps to

APRA CPS 230, ISO/IEC 42001, NIST SP 800-53, EU NIS2, SOCI Act 2018+

7Named human approval for consequential actions. Maps to EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF.

Named human approval for consequential actions, with enough context to make review real.

EU AI Act Art.14 and NIST AI RMF GOVERN-1.3 both require meaningful human oversight, and an approve/reject button with no reasoning attached does not meet it. Watch the approval rate: sustained above roughly 95% and you have automation with a liability sponge attached, which an auditor will name.

What an auditor will ask for

Approval records naming the individual, the proposed action, the reasoning and evidence shown to them, and the decision. Approval-rate statistics over time. Rejection records, which are the proof that oversight is doing work.

Build first

2. Declared autonomy level per action class

Maps to

EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, AU AI Safety Std, FDA SaMD, EU GDPR

8Irreversible actions staged. Maps to EU AI Act, ISO 42001, APRA CPS 230.

Irreversible actions staged, gated or delayed so a wrong action can be withdrawn.

Reversibility is a property of the system, not of the agent: the same delete is reversible against a versioned store and not against a live one. Most irreversible actions can be made reversible with an outbox, a soft delete or a plan/apply split, and that work is worth doing whether or not an agent is ever involved.

What an auditor will ask for

An inventory of agent-invokable actions classified reversible or not, with the mechanism named for each. For irreversible ones, either an approval gate or a documented acceptance. A test showing an action withdrawn inside the window.

Build first

2. Declared autonomy level per action class

Maps to

APRA CPS 230, ISO/IEC 42001, EU AI Act, EU DORA

9Provenance across agents. Maps to EU AI Act, ISO 42001, NIST AI RMF.

Provenance across agents: every output traceable to the upstream runs that produced its inputs.

As soon as one agent consumes another’s output, a single-run trace stops being sufficient. The question becomes which chain of reasoning produced this, and BCBS 239-style lineage expectations apply to agent outputs exactly as they do to reported figures.

What an auditor will ask for

For a given final output, the full upstream chain of agent runs that contributed to it, retrieved sources included. A demonstration that a corrected upstream input marks downstream outputs stale.

Build first

3. Full replayable trajectory

Maps to

EU AI Act, ISO/IEC 42001, NIST AI RMF, BCBS 239

10Cost measured per resolved task. Maps to ISO 42001, APRA CPS 230.

Cost measured per resolved task, not per token, with attribution to the consuming feature.

Agent cost is nonlinear in a way single-call GenAI is not: retries, fan-out and growing context mean a task can cost ten times the estimate. Cost per token is the wrong unit. The runs that fail and get retried are the ones that make the difference between a viable feature and an unviable one.

What an auditor will ask for

Cost per resolved task by agent and feature over time, alongside the failed-run cost. Evidence that spend is attributable to a product decision rather than to a shared pool.

Build first

3. Full replayable trajectory, Per-service / per-tenant cost attribution

Maps to

APRA CPS 230, ISO/IEC 42001

Tap a control for the evidence an auditor asks for and a read-only check.

Free to reuse under CC BY 4.0. These are my own views, not my employer’s, and they are not legal advice. Spotted something wrong? Email contact@hellouchit.com.

# A safety app that can’t read messages

URL: https://hellouchit.com/case-studies/ai-companion-safety.html

A parental safety app that shows AI companion screen time without reading a single message. Privacy enforced by the platform, built solo.

Work

## A safety app that can’t read messages.

Parents want to know how long their teenager spends in AI companion apps. Every existing product answers that by reading the chats. I built one that can’t.

Type

My own product

Year

2026

My role

Everything: design, code, billing, App Store

Runs on

iOS, browser extension, web

0

Messages stored, sent or readable. Anyone can check this in the extension’s permissions.

1day

The finest detail it keeps: which kind of app, for how long, on which day.

1person

Built it, from schema to subscriptions to App Store review.

This is what happens on the phone.

This is all that leaves it.

hey, you’re back! how was the test?

honestly kind of bad. i don’t want to talk about it

that’s ok. want to just hang out for a bit?

yeah. can you tell me a story

child "Sam"
day 2026-03-14
category AI companion
minutes 47

Example data. No message text, no app name, no session times. The finest detail kept is one day.

## Every monitoring app reads the chats.

AI companion apps (character chat, roleplay, synthetic partners) are a new kind of screen time for teenagers. They are private, conversational and hard to put down.

Parents mostly want to know two things: how much, and is it going up. Monitoring products answer by reading the conversations. That breaks trust between parent and child, and it creates a store of a minor’s private messages that is a liability from the moment it exists.

## Four choices that make reading impossible.

The browser extension only sees the website’s address. It maps the address to a category of app and throws the rest away. It has no permission to read pages on any monitored site, and anyone can confirm that from its manifest in a few seconds.

On iPhone, Apple’s sandbox does the enforcing. Usage data comes from Apple’s Screen Time framework, which runs in a sandbox with no network access. The app never sees exact sessions. What leaves the phone is only “this child crossed this many minutes at this time”.

The data can’t get more detailed later. Everything is stored per child, per day, per kind of app. A future request to “show the actual chats” would need a rebuild, not a settings change.

The teenager gets their own login. They see exactly what their parent sees and can add notes to a day. Products that skip this get worked around within a week.

## A shortcut I didn’t take.

The teenager’s login could have been built in a day with the database’s admin key. That key bypasses every row-level security rule, so the codebase would hold one credential able to read every family’s data.

I used locked-down database functions instead, so no such key exists anywhere in the code. The trade-off is written down too: a family code and PIN is not strong proof of identity. Eight wrong attempts lock the code for fifteen minutes, which is what makes it safe enough.

## Swift, Next.js and Postgres.

iPhone

Swift, Screen Time (DeviceActivity)

Browser

Chrome extension

Web

Next.js

Database

Postgres with row-level security

# One archival platform for 1,000+ applications

URL: https://hellouchit.com/case-studies/data-archival.html

How one AWS archival platform let a tier-1 bank retire legacy systems: 1,000+ applications, 15 TB of data and $50M+ saved every year.

Work

## One archival platform for 1,000+ applications.

A tier-1 bank in Australia and New Zealand kept old systems running only because their data had to be kept for years. We built one place to keep it, and the bank started switching the old systems off.

Client

Tier-1 bank in Australia and New Zealand

Year

2024

My role

Solution architect

Platform

AWS, built in-house

1,000+ applications. One archive.

1,000 separate archives

$50M+

Saved each year in infrastructure and running costs.

1,000+

Applications assessed and moved onto one platform.

15TB

Of structured and unstructured data under one set of retention rules.

## Old systems stayed on just to hold their data.

The bank had no shared way to archive data. Each application team had built its own, with its own tools, its own process and its own bill.

Regulation says some records must be kept for years. Because there was nowhere central to keep them, old systems stayed switched on long after anyone used them, just to hold their data.

## 1,000+ applications and every kind of data.

- Scale. More than 1,000 applications and 15 TB of data, spread across on-premises systems, other clouds and other regions.

- Mixed data. Database tables, files, documents and logs all needed the same retention, privacy and audit controls.

- Adoption. Application teams had to choose to move. If getting data back out was slow or awkward, they wouldn’t.

## One AWS platform, rolled out by data type.

We spent three months assessing all 1,000+ applications before designing anything. We compared off-the-shelf products against a custom build on data patterns, compliance needs and cost. A custom AWS platform won.

We rolled it out by type of data rather than by application: structured data first, then documents and files. Retention, expiry and deletion run automatically. Teams get their data back through self-service, with access controlled by their existing Active Directory groups.

The bank’s own team runs it. We handed over full design documents, runbooks and review processes.

Sources

On-premises systems

Other clouds and regions

1,000+ applications

Move and process

AWS DataSync

AWS Lambda

Step Functions orchestration

Automated classification

Archive

Amazon S3

MongoDB Atlas metadata

Alation lineage

Retention, expiry, purge

Get it back

Self-service retrieval dashboard

Access by AD group

Business and audit users

How data moves from source systems into the archive and back out to the teams who need it. Everything is built with Terraform and deployed through CI/CD.

## Four decisions that made it work.

- Three months of discovery before any design. We looked at data volumes, formats, retention rules and regulatory limits for every application, then built decision trees to choose between cloud services, an enterprise product and a custom build.

- One platform for every data type. A single application often holds tables, files and documents. Handling all of them in one place meant an application could be switched off in one go.

- Roll out by data type. Structured data first, then semi-structured and unstructured. Each phase was harder than the last, and the team learned on the easier one.

- Ship the operating model, not just the platform. Onboarding guides, runbooks, security documentation and review processes, so new applications could join without us.

# Loans paid out in under five minutes

URL: https://hellouchit.com/case-studies/digital-lending.html

A digital lending platform for a leading Asian bank: loans paid out in under five minutes, live in six months with 200+ engineers.

Work

## Loans paid out in under five minutes.

A leading Asian bank wanted a new lending platform that could approve a loan and pay it out within five minutes, for millions of customers, launched in six months.

Client

Leading Asian bank

Years

2021 to 2022

My role

Delivery lead and technical architect

Team

200+ people in 50+ squads

<5min

From application to money paid out.

6months

To production, on the date agreed at the start.

0

Critical incidents at go-live, across 50+ regulated AWS environments.

## Five minutes, six months, one regulated bank.

The bank’s existing lending process took far longer than five minutes. It wanted a new platform built on Pega for workflow, Go microservices and the FIS risk engine, running on AWS under strict banking rules.

Six months is not enough time to run discovery, design, build and test one after another. Everything had to happen in parallel.

## Five minutes, start to finish.

5:00

- Customer applies on mobile or web

- Pega runs the workflow

- FIS risk engine scores the credit

- Loan approved

- Money paid out

Paid out inside the limit.

## 200 people, 50 environments, two languages.

- Team size. We had to hire and organise more than 200 people across several skill areas, fast.

- Environments. More than 50 regulated AWS environments had to support parallel development, testing and release without teams blocking each other.

- Language. Many of the bank’s stakeholders worked in their own language. Misunderstandings were a real delivery risk.

- New patterns. Running Pega with cloud DevOps in a regulated bank had no standard playbook. We had to design one that would pass audit.

## Squads built around the platform.

Three kinds of leadership group worked side by side: delivery leads who owned timelines and dependencies, architects who owned Pega, the risk engine, the microservices and integration, and a PMO group that owned planning, reporting and risk.

Squads were organised around parts of the platform and business capabilities, not around the org chart. We hired for specific skills across Asia rather than for job titles, and set each task’s timeline by the skills of the person doing it.

The bank’s local PMO teams were paired with ours in each region, so decisions happened in the stakeholders’ own language.

Engineering basics were fixed from the start: automated testing, containers everywhere, and mandatory code and pipeline reviews.

Channels

Mobile app

Web

Millions of customers

Front end

Front-end microservices

Decide

Pega workflow and decisions

FIS risk engine

Serve

Go microservices

Disbursement

AWS, 50+ regulated environments, containers and CI/CD throughout

How an application moves from the customer’s phone to a payout.

## What I’d tell the next team.

- Regulation doesn’t have to mean slow. With the right architecture, automation and governance, a regulated bank moved at startup speed.

- Past about 150 people, structure is what keeps it working. Leadership groups and squads stopped the programme turning into chaos.

- DevOps has to come first. Without automation, containers and CI/CD, 50+ environments would have slowed everyone down.

- Plan by skill, not by job title. Setting each task’s timeline by the person doing it made delivery far more predictable.

- Talk in the client’s language. Local PMO teams made decisions faster and built trust.

# Agent readiness check

URL: https://hellouchit.com/tools/agent-readiness.html

Ten questions, two minutes: score how ready your AI agents are for a regulated environment and see the three things to fix first. Nothing leaves your browser.

Ten controls for AI agents

## Agent readiness check.

Ten questions, one for each control. Answer for what is actually enforced today, not what the design document says. It takes about two minutes and nothing leaves your browser.

## 

Back

See all ten questions

- 
Identity. What identity does the agent act under?

- A human’s credentials, usually whoever deployed it.

- A shared service account used by several agents or jobs.

- Its own service account, but with a long-lived static key.

- Its own federated workload identity; no static credentials in the execution path.

- Own federated identity, and a revocation test on record showing tool calls fail within one polling interval.

- 
Autonomy level. Is autonomy declared per action class, or per agent?

- Not declared. The agent does what it can do.

- Described in a design doc; nothing enforces it.

- A register of action classes exists with levels assigned and an approver named.

- Levels are enforced at execution, not just documented.

- Enforced at execution and the level in force is recorded per run, so you can answer what it was allowed to do then.

- 
Trajectory. Can you replay a specific run from step N?

- Final output is logged. Nothing else.

- Prompts and responses logged; tool calls are not.

- Tool calls logged with arguments and results.

- Full run exported: assembled context, retrieved document IDs, every call, model and prompt version, tokens, cost, latency.

- All of that, and replay from an arbitrary step is a tested capability rather than a claim.

- 
Injection defence. Is retrieved and tool-returned content treated as data or as instructions?

- Not considered. Retrieved text goes straight into the prompt.

- Direct user input is filtered; retrieved and tool-returned content is not.

- Some structural separation between instructions and data.

- Indirect injection red-teamed through retrieval paths as well as direct input.

- Every retrieval and tool-result path red-teamed on a schedule, with structural separation enforced and regression tests for known payloads.

- 
Tool authorisation. Where is the boundary on what the agent may do?

- The system prompt tells it what not to do.

- A tool list exists, the same for every context and role.

- Tools scoped per role, defined in configuration.

- A policy engine outside the model authorises each invocation.

- Policy engine authorises each call and decision logs show allow and deny with a reason, exportable per role.

- 
Human oversight. What does approval of a consequential action actually involve?

- No approval step.

- An approve/reject button with the proposed action and nothing else.

- Approval shows the reasoning and the evidence the agent used.

- As above, and approvals are recorded with the named individual and their decision.

- All of that, plus the approval rate is monitored. Sustained near 100% is treated as a finding, not a success.

- 
Blast radius. What stops a loop, and has it been tested mid-run?

- Nothing. A loop runs until someone notices the bill.

- A step limit in code; no spend or rate ceiling.

- Step, spend and rate ceilings configured per agent.

- Ceilings configured and a kill switch exists.

- Kill switch tested stopping an agent mid-run, with the time from decision to stop recorded.

- 
Reversibility. How are irreversible actions handled?

- The agent calls whatever the tool does. Reversibility was never assessed.

- Known-dangerous actions are excluded from the tool list.

- Agent-invokable actions inventoried and classified reversible or not.

- Irreversible ones carry an approval gate or a delay window.

- Classified, gated, and the reversal mechanism is named and exercised for each: versioned store, compensating transaction or delay.

- 
Provenance. When one agent consumes another’s output, can you trace the chain?

- Single agent only, or chains are not traced.

- Each agent logs its own run; the join across them is manual.

- Outputs carry the upstream run ID that produced them.

- For a given output, the full upstream chain including retrieved sources is retrievable.

- Full chain retrievable, and a corrected upstream input marks the downstream outputs that depended on it.

- 
Cost per outcome. What unit is agent cost measured in?

- Not measured separately from the platform bill.

- Total tokens or total spend, unattributed.

- Cost per run, attributed to an agent.

- Cost per resolved task, attributed to the consuming feature.

- Cost per resolved task with failed-run cost tracked alongside it, so retries and fan-out are visible rather than absorbed.

Also available as JSON.
